tagline: Creek Road reaches a reservoir built to restrain Sandy Creek’s floods
intro: Lake Wilhelm Scenic Byway follows Creek Road in Mercer County through part of Maurice K. Goddard State Park. The reservoir shares its shores with the park and adjoining state game lands. PennDOT records the byway designation as effective in 2006; Visit Pennsylvania highlights the lake’s appeal to anglers and boaters.

The landscape came first from a flood-control project. Repeated Sandy Creek flooding prompted a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers study in 1939, but World War II delayed plans. State and local authorities worked together to advance a dam and recreation facilities. Land acquisition followed in the late 1960s, the dam was completed in 1971, and the park opened in 1972. The park was named for Maurice K. Goddard, whose work for Pennsylvania expanded its state park system. His goal was a park within 25 miles of every resident, and this reservoir became one of the state’s recreation landscapes.

Follow the corridor along Creek Road, numbered SR 1019, toward its endpoint at PA 173. Within the park, the lake, woods and old fields support different bird communities: migrating waterfowl use the water in spring and fall, while pileated woodpeckers inhabit the woods.

moments.title: Sandy Creek dam
moments.text: The dam that created Lake Wilhelm was completed in 1971, more than three decades after the flood study began. Recurring floods on Sandy Creek had led the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to begin studying the problem in 1939. World War II delayed the plans. State, county, township and municipal authorities later worked together to advance both flood control and recreation. The resulting reservoir occupies land shared by the state park and adjoining game lands. Land was acquired in the late 1960s, construction followed, and the public park opened in 1972, the year after the dam was finished.

moments.title: Lake Wilhelm marina
moments.text: Lake Wilhelm is a warm-water fishery, with largemouth and smallmouth bass, walleye, northern pike and muskellunge among its game fish. Bald eagles and osprey can be seen over the lake searching the water for fish. Spring and fall bring another use of the reservoir: migrating waterfowl stop here, including loons, goldeneyes, mergansers and buffleheads. The marina has a building and boat launches. The park’s old fields and forests also support woodcocks, nighthawks, snipes and warblers, extending the bird habitat beyond the open water. Perch, crappie, bluegill and catfish join the lake’s larger game fish.

moments.title: Maurice K. Goddard State Park
moments.text: Pileated woodpeckers inhabit the park’s woods, while bluebirds and purple martins use its old fields and meadows. Those habitats belong to a park that opened in 1972 and bears the name of Pennsylvania conservation official Maurice K. Goddard. Goddard had worked at Mont Alto Forestry School and Penn State before taking the state post; he retired after 24 years working for Pennsylvania’s parks. As Secretary of the Bureau of Forests and Waters, Goddard pursued a state park within 25 miles of every Pennsylvania resident. By his retirement in 1979, he had helped add 45 parks to the state system.
